size: New AI data centers and expansions; no applications currently on file
reason: Adopted as a public health and safety urgency ordinance to close a zoning gap: staff will develop land use and zoning regulations limiting impacts on public safety, city services, energy and water; proactive, with findings due Oct. 10

size: All data center development town-wide
developer: N/A (no developer has approached the town)
reason: Proactive, official-led pause adopted after learning nearby towns had already been contacted by developers; the town will hold monthly public information sessions while it studies energy, water and zoning impacts

size: Large-scale data centers county-wide
developer: N/A (no developer has approached the county)
reason: Complete regulatory gap: the judge-executive said the county has no zoning rules to review a data center if one arrived, so the Fiscal Court paused development while it builds oversight rules covering energy and water impacts

size: Data center development within city limits (does not extend to the rest of Clark County)
reason: Commission proactively paused development to study energy, water and land use impacts and gather public input before any project is permitted

size: New data center applications city-wide; the former McKinley Paper mill site is zoned heavy industrial
reason: Electric rates, water use, industrial land supply, noise and environmental quality; council directed staff to draft a moratorium to close a filing window before new rules take effect, with Planning Commission and Utility Advisory Committee input

size: Future data centers; the Google-backed $832M 'Project Maize' would be exempt
reason: Residents raised air quality, chemical and health impacts and said the existing project was approved without adequate research; grassroots pressure prompted the Common Council to discuss pausing future development

size: Data centers; limits on facility size and proximity to residential and agricultural land
reason: Land use compatibility near homes and farmland after strong resident pressure; supervisors adopted permanent zoning limits on size and setbacks, with noise and water amendments still before the planning commission. No pause is in effect

size: All permits for data centers in the village
reason: Regulatory and zoning gap amid Ohio's rapid data center buildout; council proactively paused permits to study what village rules should be in place, framing it as preparation rather than a stance against the industry

duration: 1 year, renews annually unless council acts
size: New data centers larger than 21,780 sq ft (about half an acre) within the city and the 1.5-mile extraterritorial zoning area
reason: Residents and council members raised questions about water, environment, health, power costs, city services and municipal finances; the pause gives the city time to study costs, benefits and impacts before accepting applications

size: Citywide prohibition on data centers including AI facilities; would apply to land now in the city and to future annexations
reason: Water and electricity consumption for very few jobs, argued by Mayor Jerry Dyer and Councilmember Richardson; official-led, with council directing staff to draft and define a 10-year prohibition in the Development Code and a parallel push to make data center nondisclosure agreements public

duration: Permanent ban on the Nov 3, 2026 ballot
size: Charter amendment banning construction of new data centers city-wide
reason: Grassroots petition drive: five residents circulated a charter-amendment petition over land use and utility concerns, council rejected their signature count, and the Ohio Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Sept. 1 that voters must decide, after which council passed an emergency ordinance placing it on the ballot
vote: Emergency ordinance (placed on ballot after court order)

size: All data centers county-wide; the same ordinance also bans landfills and large battery energy storage systems
developer: N/A (no developer had pitched a project)
reason: Farmland and rural land use: the Fiscal Court chose an outright ban over a moratorium after hearing near-universal resident opposition, citing preservation of Thoroughbred horse farms, historic agriculture and a finite land supply, and pointing to the divisive hyperscale fight in nearby Burgin as what it wanted to avoid; grassroots-driven sentiment, enacted proactively by officials

size: Data centers, large-scale data centers and large load customer facilities in unincorporated areas; telecom, public safety and previously approved projects exempt
reason: Electricity and water demand on a county wholly dependent on the Floridan Aquifer, plus noise, vibration, lighting, heat, construction traffic, roads and emergency services; commissioners directed staff in June to draft the pause (official-led) against a backdrop of a resident petition, with a water and infrastructure study due back by Aug. 2027

size: Medium-scale (2,000-5,000 servers, 5-49 MW) and large-scale (50 MW or more monthly peak load) data centers

size: Data centers, bitcoin and cryptocurrency mining, server farms and similar technology uses; MW thresholds to be set during the pause
developer: N/A (no project proposed near the city)
reason: Water consumption, noise and the electrical burden on existing ratepayers of city-owned Riviera Utilities; a proactive, official-led pause with no application pending, making Foley roughly the ninth Alabama city to adopt one

size: Data centers and energy facilities township-wide; no application pending
developer: N/A for data centers (adjacent dispute is RWE Americas' 200 MW Silver Maple Solar project)
reason: Zoning and local control: the board repealed its earlier data-center-only moratorium and adopted a broader one covering energy facilities so it can finish updating the master plan and renewable energy ordinance, explicitly to defend local planning authority against state preemption under PA 233; official-led, reinforced by organized resident opposition to the neighboring solar project

size: New data center and fossil-fuel power plant applications township-wide; only 52 parcels are zoned heavy or light industrial
developer: Nadara (right-to-purchase agreement on 800 acres near Gans)
reason: Noise, setbacks and land use compatibility: supervisors tabled two detailed ordinances to meet state notice requirements and adopted a resolution barring any data center or power plant application in the interim so nothing could be filed in the gap; official-led drafting triggered by Nadara's land deal, with about 40 residents attending in opposition

size: All data center proposals; ends by-right approval in general industrial zones
reason: Zoning and land use, energy demand and ratepayer bill impacts: staff-recommended zoning text amendment requiring a conditional use permit for every data center, citing JLARC findings on construction impacts, limited long-term jobs and incompatibility near homes; official-led, and no pause is in effect, though the mayor said it could slow applications to a halt

duration: 1 year (first reading; two more readings required)
size: New applications, permits, rezonings and incentives for data centers, cryptocurrency mining and data-processing facilities in unincorporated areas
reason: Water, electricity, noise and environmental impacts, plus a zoning gap that currently permits data centers in several commercial and industrial districts; official-led and explicitly pre-emptive, with strong resident support for preserving the county's rural character, and the pending ordinance doctrine adopted alongside to stop a rush of filings

size: New data centers city-wide; follows a 60-day application pause adopted July 28, 2026
developer: N/A (driver is Meta's existing hyperscale campus in the city)
reason: Noise complaints from neighbors of the Meta campus and water and electric utility impacts, plus the need to distinguish server closets and edge facilities from hyperscale projects in the zoning code; council-led with resident support, after the planning commission recommended the pause 5-2

size: Council actions supporting data centers: rezonings, annexations, property sales, contracts and tax abatements; city planning staff work and the existing Google campus are unaffected
developer: Google ($2B campus, exempt and already operational)
reason: Public health, environmental, infrastructure and resource demands raised by residents of the southeast-side district that hosts the Google campus; a councilwoman's ordinance pairs the pause with a nine-member Community Infrastructure and Environmental Review Commission, and a rival task-force proposal was withdrawn in its favor

size: New AI data center applications county-wide; the land development code has no data center language, so they are implicitly allowed under industrial zoning
reason: Water and energy: the vice mayor's report cites a projected 96-million-gallon-per-day groundwater shortfall by 2045 for a utility wholly dependent on groundwater, plus AI facility power draw comparable to 100,000 homes and up to 5 million gallons of water a day, and the land footprint of typical campuses; official-led, framed as a timeout to write zoning rules rather than an anti-business measure

size: Large data centers county-wide; the disclosed project is 32 natural gas engines totaling about 300 MW near Hachita and Playas
developer: Site Layer 1, LLC (sole listed address is an empty Manhattan office floor)
reason: Air quality, emissions, water and energy, compounded by secrecy: residents only learned of the gas-fired project through an air-permit legal notice in the local paper, and a commissioner responded by proposing a pause modeled on Socorro County's ordinance; grassroots-triggered, with the state environment secretary also criticizing the developer's minimal community engagement

duration: Permanent ban (proposed; planning board hearing Sept 15, 2026)
size: All data centers across the township's 38 square miles; accessory server rooms inside existing buildings still permitted up to 10% of floor space or 2,000 sq ft
reason: Land use and industrial scale: officials withdrew an earlier ban ordinance and reintroduced it as Ordinance 26-32 after the planning board asked for an accessory server room definition, keeping data centers defined separately from warehouses and barring flex space or research buildings from conversion; official-led, following a non-binding resolution opposing data centers that attorneys said carried no legal weight

duration: Permanent ban on the Jan 5, 2027 special election ballot
size: Charter amendment barring data centers with combined monthly demand above 25 MW from any energy source
reason: Grassroots petition drive over energy demand and land use: residents gathered signatures (133 of 180 validated) but council could not muster a quorum in the two-day window after certification, missing the Nov. 3 ballot, so at a special meeting it set a January special election at roughly $15,000 cost; mirrors the 25 MW template used in other Ohio communities

duration: 30 days, extended to 180 days on Aug 6, 2026
size: Any data-center-related application or permit request in unincorporated Walker County
developer: N/A named (a disputed site on Bulldog Drive prompted county clarifications)
reason: Zoning and land use compatibility, water and electricity demand, noise, lighting, buffers and setbacks; official-led, with a Data Center Development Standards Study Committee meeting every other Thursday before drawing more than 40 residents, weighing closed-loop cooling, water caps and distance from homes, with zoning amendments expected in early 2027

size: Large-scale data centers in unincorporated Escambia County, outside the City of Pensacola and the Town of Century; accessory server rooms at hospitals, universities and employers remain allowed
reason: Water and energy demand and land use incompatibility: commissioners passed an outright ordinance ban on top of a July resolution memorializing that the Land Development Code already excludes data centers, after more than two dozen residents asked them to harden the language against legal challenge; a follow-on 12-month moratorium was abandoned on Sept. 10 when the county attorney advised it would weaken, not strengthen, the existing ban

duration: Permanent ban on the Nov 3, 2026 ballot
size: Zoning amendment prohibiting any facility with an aggregate data center area of 25,000 sq ft or larger
reason: Land use and industrial scale: the select board deliberately skipped a temporary moratorium in June, reasoning a straight zoning prohibition could take effect sooner, and approved ballot language defining and banning data centers; official-led with no recorded opposition from residents or officials, alongside a companion comprehensive plan growth-area amendment

size: Concept plans, site development plans and permits for data centers and office data processing facilities
reason: Water and aquifer protection, energy demand and land use near homes and schools: three council members' memo sought a pause, but a special session left the council split four for, three undecided and four against, with staff recommending Unified Development Code amendments instead; the active track prohibits data centers over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone and imposes 500-foot setbacks from schools, daycares, hospitals and homes
vote: No vote taken (council split at special session)

size: A tiered 'High Infrastructure Impact Development' framework keyed to electricity, water, wastewater, road and emergency-service demand, with annual projected-versus-actual usage reporting
reason: Infrastructure capacity, water and energy: council directed the planning and zoning commission to keep developing an impact-based ordinance rather than a pause, deliberately written around infrastructure demand rather than naming the industry, while the city separately weighs extraterritorial zoning up to two miles out; official-led following a public input process on AI data centers. No moratorium is in effect

size: Roughly 1,000 acres of CM-2 land near Triboro Industrial Park, about 29% of the borough
developer: Triboro Commerce Park LLC and ERCOR Triboro (Sansone Group), which bought 500 acres for $80M and proposes nine data centers
reason: Grassroots opposition over transparency, health, water, wildlife, property values and utility costs, organized as Stop Olyphant Data Centers with more than 1,600 members: council rejected a data center zoning amendment 4-3 and declared a curative amendment giving it 180 days to rewrite the zoning, but the window ended early when council voted 6-0 on June 9 to settle a developer lawsuit and stipulate that its initial vote had validly adopted the zoning

12-month moratorium failed twice: May 27 attempt fell short after a vote-tally error (corrected 8-6-1); weakened version exempting AVAIO Digital's Wrightsville project rejected 10-3 on Jul 28 after critics called the carve-out a 'free pass'; amendment to close it also failed. First Texas county moratorium (enacted May 12, 3-2) rescinded unanimously June 4 after RCM Hill LLC filed a $100M federal suit (May 27) alleging the county exceeded its lawful powers and threatened grid interconnection; county adopted a developer review checklist (water, traffic, noise, public notice) instead. Federal suit remains active.
County committee declined to pursue a data center moratorium after being advised of legal limits on county zoning authority; residents continue pushing for action.
City Commission again voted down a 6-month data center moratorium and gave final approval to data center regulations after a 4.5-hour, standing-room-only meeting June 16.

Seven-month statewide DC moratorium proposal voted down on session's final day; legislature instead passed HB 233 (DCs first cut off in blackout), HB 445 (developers must self-supply power within 10 years), SB 326 (Delmarva Power billing limits and audits)
Commissioners voted down proposed 6-month moratorium on new DC proposals while weighing Project Delta (January rezoning voided by court in April over defective public notice; developer to resubmit)

Proposed constitutional amendment to ban data centers over 25 MW failed to qualify for the 2026 ballot, gathering ~70,000 of 413,488 signatures needed by the July 1 deadline; backers plan a 2027 retry

City Council voted 2-4 against a one-year data center moratorium on its third reading despite months of resident pressure; a separate ballot measure capping data centers at 25 MW advances to a third reading and possible special election
Commission declined a data center moratorium and adopted a 72-hour disclosure policy for data center proposals instead, promoting transparency without pausing development
Township board rejected a proposed six-month moratorium; residents threatened a recall campaign in response

City Council voted down a one-year moratorium, clearing the way for a Google data center on ~900 annexed acres after the Salix Guardian Alliance and 100+ residents pushed for impact studies; a councilmember flipped after Google was named. Woodbury County's suit over the annexation remains pending.

A staff-drafted six-month moratorium failed on a 3-3 tie with one commissioner absent, after residents spoke in favor citing water, electrical infrastructure and noise; opponents argued a pause would close off economic opportunity. No data center project is currently targeting the county.

Council repealed its six-month moratorium 7-0 (Resolution 2026-47) to coincide with a new ordinance making data centers a special land use in M-1/M-2 only, with residential setbacks, noise limits and decommissioning rules. Wixom Industrial One LLC's federal suit over the pause (filed Aug 7) remains active.

City Commission voted down a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers and a companion definition ordinance, with the majority accepting staff's view that the land development code already bars data centers. Leon County unanimously adopted an 18-month moratorium a month later.

Village Council voted 4-1 against a moratorium on hyperscale data center applications, saying it wanted new legal counsel to draft language that could survive a court challenge; the council then fired the village manager and removed the village attorney the same night as residents pressed for safeguards on 'Project Growler' and 'Project Beskar'

City rejected citizen petitions for a 25 MW data center ban charter amendment over signature validity and refused a refile before the Sept. 4 ballot deadline; organizers say 276 of 220 required signatures were verified and must now restart the drive

Commission took no action on hearings for a 12-month moratorium on mid-sized (10-50 MW) data centers after the county attorney advised the Land Development Code and August ordinance already ban them outright; a moratorium was seen as weakening the existing ban
